title: Cu–Zn–In–S · Cu:Zn = 1:20 at 210 °C

conflictPairs.context: Preserve supplier wording and Methods wording separately. Printed mass and mole are internally inconsistent; neither is corrected.

Keep the Methods sequence exactly (initial 210 °C until clear, sulfur injection, selected 150/180/210/240 °C hold, then 230 °C for 5 min). Figure 3A first trace is 150 °C and agrees with Figures 1D, 2, and 4. The Methods do not explain the temperature transitions (including how the 150 °C hold follows the 210 °C preheat) or ramp rates; do not invent a monotonic or corrected sequence.
Actual SI labels HRTEM S4; S2 is In2S3 absorption/XRD. Bind to actual caption and preserve the mismatch.
TEM A–C are three explicit specimens; Figure1D and Figure2 show four temperatures including 150 °C. The three-sample prose does not explain the extra 150 °C XRD/EDS trace.
S5/Table S1 captions say “obtained under different reaction temperatures” but visible legend/columns are Cu/Zn ratios. Main text links these to composition series EDX; preserve caption mismatch.

The printed prose reports 620–750 nm for 2.0–7.0 nm particles. Figure 3B visually presents the same trend but its plotted endpoints do not map exactly to the prose range. Preserve this qualitative graph/prose discrepancy only; no digitized point values or new numeric rows are supported.

intuition.title: Authors’ temperature rationale
intuition.summary: The authors state that reaction temperatures above 140 °C were needed to form homogeneous Cu–Zn–In–S nuclei and to avoid Cu₂S, In₂S₃ and ZnS impurities. This is their stated design rationale, not a universal temperature threshold or proof that every reported sample is impurity-free.
intuition.scope: Source-attributed rationale for the material family; comparison data and individual route outcomes remain distinct.

general_background.title: An indium carboxylate feed
general_background.summary: Oleic acid can exchange with acetate when preparing an indium carboxylate feed for colloidal phosphide growth. The carboxylate environment affects how molecular intermediates and particle surfaces accommodate indium.
general_background.label: General background, not the authors' interpretation

reference.title: Two-Step Nucleation and Growth of InP Quantum Dots via Magic-Sized Cluster Intermediates

general_background.title: Oleylamine changes how sulfur is delivered
general_background.summary: An amine can convert elemental sulfur into soluble polysulfide species before metal sulfide nanocrystals form. How sulfur is made available from that solution affects whether new nuclei form or existing particles keep growing.
general_background.label: General background, not the authors' interpretation

reference.title: From Sulfur−Amine Solutions to Metal Sulfide Nanocrystals: Peering into the Oleylamine−Sulfur Black Box

general_background.title: Octadecene is not always inert
general_background.summary: Octadecene provides a weakly coordinating medium for hot solution growth, leaving the ligands more freedom to control surface binding. It can also polymerize under growth conditions, leaving an alkene-derived residue that is difficult to separate from hydrophobic nanocrystals.
general_background.label: General background, not the authors' interpretation

reference.title: The Trouble with ODE: Polymerization during Nanocrystal Synthesis

general_background.title: A thiol can both supply sulfur and bind the surface
general_background.summary: In metal-sulfide routes that use an alkanethiol as the sulfur feed, metal–thiolate chemistry can supply sulfur to the growing lattice. Thiol or thiolate species can also bind at the particle surface, so sulfur delivery and surface capping may be linked.
general_background.label: General background, not the authors' interpretation
